Fanny Crosby
FAN-ee KROZ-bee
proper noun
Fanny, a familiar form of Frances, “free one”; Crosby, an English place-name, “dwelling by the cross.”

📖 Biblical Definition

Frances Jane Crosby (1820–1915) was a blind American hymn-writer who composed near eight thousand sacred songs, becoming one of the most beloved hymnists in the history of the English-speaking church. Blinded in infancy through a careless treatment, she never bewailed her loss but counted it a mercy, saying she would not have had it otherwise, for the first face she would ever see would be the face of her Saviour. Out of that settled joy flowed hymns of assurance and praise that have carried generations to Christ: “Blessed Assurance,” “To God Be the Glory,” “Pass Me Not, O Gentle Saviour,” “Rescue the Perishing,” and “All the Way My Saviour Leads Me.” Her verse is plain, warm, and Christ-exalting, fixed upon the cross, the blood, and the believer’s glad hope of heaven. Working closely with gospel musicians, she would often receive a tune and within minutes furnish words wedded to it. Crosby labored among the poor of New York’s missions, refusing to live in comfort while souls perished. The believer honors her as a faithful witness whose darkness God turned to the church’s lasting song, a living proof that affliction borne in faith becomes an instrument of praise. “This is my story, this is my song,” she wrote, “praising my Saviour all the day long.”

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A blind American hymn-writer of near eight thousand songs whose Christ-exalting verse has carried generations to assurance and praise.

FANNY CROSBY, blind American hymn-writer (1820–1915) of some eight thousand sacred songs.

Author of “Blessed Assurance,” “To God Be the Glory,” and “Pass Me Not, O Gentle Saviour.”

Counted her blindness a mercy, longing first to see the face of Christ.

Labored among the poor in New York’s rescue missions.

Her hymns fix the heart upon the cross, the blood, and the hope of heaven (Eph 1:7).

📖 Key Scripture

Eph 1:7 — "In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace;"

Psa 146:8 — "The LORD openeth the eyes of the blind: the LORD raiseth them that are bowed down: the LORD loveth the righteous:"

Heb 10:22 — "Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with pure water."

Psa 34:3 — "O magnify the LORD with me, and let us exalt his name together."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Crosby’s hymns of true assurance are sometimes thinned into vague feeling-songs; the cure is to keep her words anchored where she set them, in the blood and righteousness of Christ.

expand to see more

The corruption that touches Crosby’s legacy is the modern habit of singing her hymns as warm sentiment cut loose from doctrine. “Blessed Assurance” is gutted when assurance is made a mood rather than the Spirit’s witness grounded in Christ’s finished work; “To God Be the Glory” is hollowed when the glory of the cross is replaced by the worshipper’s own experience. Crosby herself never meant her songs as self-expression but as testimony to a real Redeemer and a real redemption by His blood.

The lesson to recover is that genuine assurance is doctrinal joy, not manufactured feeling. Crosby’s blindness taught her to walk by faith and not by sight, and her hymns teach the church to rest its confidence on what God has done, not on what the heart happens to feel. Sing her words as she wrote them, full of blood and cross and the sure hope of seeing the Saviour’s face, and they remain a faithful witness.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Her name joins “free one” with “dwelling by the cross,” an apt emblem of a soul set free at the cross.

expand to see more

Fanny Crosby — Frances, “free one”; Crosby, “dwelling by the cross.”

Hymn, from the Greek hymnos, a song of praise to God.

Assurance, from Latin ad-securus, “made safe,” the settled confidence of faith.

She often wrote under many pen-names so her vast output would not seem the work of one hand.

“Pass Me Not” she drew from the cry of the blind beggar at Jericho (Luk 18:38).

Usage

"Fanny Crosby wrote near eight thousand hymns though she never saw a printed page."

"We sang Fanny Crosby’s “Blessed Assurance” at the close of the service."

"Fanny Crosby counted her blindness a mercy, longing first to see the face of her Saviour."
